proposals.text: The powers — knowledge, memory, removal — have been established.
But a power needs a support, and the question is what supports them.
Kārikā 1 gives the support's own form in the image of the pratibhā: the flashing that runs through the ordered word-objects, seasoned with their order, touched by it — but itself not ordered.
Its support is therefore not anything ordered, but the order-less, infinite-consciousness-form knower.
And that knower is the great Lord.
The point of kārikā 1 is to establish that the support has this form — order-less, conscious, free — before the following verses prove that it exists by presence-and-absence.
The passage does not by itself prove that all such order-less supports are numerically one; the unity is argued later.
The objection is straightforward: if reflexive awareness is joined to linguistic form, why is it not simply a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)?
Abhinavagupta answers by asking what construction actually does.
The forms considered involve combining, differentiating, or determining contents.
The awareness expressed as "I," however, is not treated as one more relation constructed between independently given elements.

The point is therefore not merely that the "I" is linguistically unusual; it is that linguistic articulation does not show that the underlying self-awareness is itself produced by conceptual determination.
This allows Abhinavagupta to preserve a distinction between reflexive self-awareness and the conceptual operations that articulate it.
The stronger Śaiva conclusion — that this self-awareness belongs ultimately to a single universal subject — is not established by this passage alone and depends on arguments elsewhere.

The claim is that the essence of light is the reflexive awareness, not the bare showing of objects.
The crystal supplies the contrast: a light that merely showed the world without knowing that it showed it would be no different from crystal — it would reflect, but be inert.
What makes the light conscious is the self-awareness in the very act of manifesting.
The passage then identifies this self-knowing with the supreme speech (parā-vāk) and with the Lord's freedom and lordship.
The identification with the Word is the extension: the reflexivity is not a bare self-presence but the supreme speech from which the lower levels of language descend.
This is why the word-joined "I" need not be a construction — language is the form the self-grasp takes, not something that produces it.
The passage establishes the reflexivity claim; the full account of the powers and the Lordship is developed in the following vimarśas.
The sharpest objection to the unity: if consciousness is one and the difference of things is mere ignorance, how is action possible?
For action needs an agent and an object, distinct; but if all is one, there is no distinct object.
Abhinavagupta first answers with the will-to-do — the single re-recollection marked by the will that joins the agent and the object.
Then he challenges the premise that the difference is ignorance.
If the difference were an "un-explainable" ignorance, of whom would it be?

The one-form reality cannot have an ignorance that presupposes a duality to be absent from; the separate souls cannot bear it, since they are supposed to be produced by it; and "un-explainable" is a refusal to answer, not an answer.
The difference is real: cognition rests in difference as it does not rest in non-difference.
The passage establishes that the difference cannot be an un-explainable ignorance.
The full positive account of the difference (as the self's own manifestation) is developed elsewhere.
